questions.q: Why do applications pool database connections instead of opening one per request?
options: Pools encrypt traffic with TLS that raw connections would otherwise leave in plaintext
Connection setup and auth are costly; pooling reuses live connections
Databases refuse concurrent connections from a single client IP
Pooling upgrades every request to a prepared transaction

questions.q: A request needs a connection but the pool is fully checked out. What typically happens?
options: The pool opens a temporary superuser connection to serve it
The pool silently cancels the oldest currently running query
The request gets rerouted automatically to a read replica with spare connection capacity
The request queues until a connection frees or a timeout fires

questions.q: For a CPU-bound database workload, a good starting pool size is closest to...
options: a small multiple of the database server's core count
one connection per concurrent end user of the application
whatever max_connections allows, minus a small safety margin
ten connections for every application server instance deployed

questions.q: In PgBouncer, what does transaction pooling mode mean?
options: Each client keeps one server connection for its entire session
Every transaction is mirrored synchronously to a standby server
A server connection is lent out only for each transaction's duration
Each individual SQL statement gets its own server connection assignment

questions.q: Which symptom points to pool exhaustion rather than a slow database?
options: High CPU utilization on the database host itself
All queries slowing uniformly across every connected service as the database saturates
Rising disk I/O wait times on the primary storage node
Requests stall before any SQL runs, then hit checkout timeouts

questions.q: Why do serverless functions clash with traditional connection pooling?
options: Serverless runtimes cannot hold outbound TCP sockets open at all
Every concurrent instance brings its own pool, multiplying connections
Functions cannot participate safely in database transactions
Pools need writable local disk that serverless platforms forbid

questions.q: A pooled connection turns out to be dead at checkout. What should the pool do?
options: Return it to the idle set for the next caller to try again
Trigger an application restart to rebuild all connections cleanly
Discard it, open a replacement, and hand that out transparently
Fail the request, since broken connections cannot be replaced

questions.q: What does a pool's idle timeout govern?
options: How long an unused connection stays open before being closed
How long a statement may execute before cancellation triggers
How long a caller waits in the checkout queue before erroring
How long a transaction may remain open before forced rollback

questions.q: After a deploy, acquisition timeouts spike though query latency is unchanged. Most likely cause?
options: The database filesystem is silently running out of space
The new build leaks prepared statements on every single call
New code holds connections longer per request, starving the pool
The deploy disabled TCP keepalives on the pooler

questions.q: 30 app instances each run a 20-connection pool against max_connections=200. Core risk?
options: Bursts can attempt 600 connections and get refused at the database
Postgres load-balances the excess connections across backends so only latency rises slightly
Idle pools will crash the WAL writer under memory pressure
Each instance gets automatically capped at six connections

questions.q: Which application feature breaks under transaction-mode pooling?
options: Multi-statement transactions committed as one atomic unit
Single-statement autocommit reads issued under heavy load
Row-level security policies evaluated on every query
Session state like temp tables, SET values, and advisory locks

questions.q: A nightly batch saturates the shared pool and starves the API. Reasonable mitigation?
options: Raise max_connections by an order of magnitude during the batch window
Give the batch its own capped pool or point it at a replica
Shorten the API's checkout timeout so it fails faster
Run the batch on raw unpooled connections instead

questions.q: Why is simply enlarging the pool often the wrong fix for checkout timeouts?
options: A saturated database gains contention, not throughput, from extra connections
Pool sizes are fixed at process start and cannot ever change
Larger pools break connection validation on most database drivers
Beyond 100 connections, poolers switch to statement mode automatically

questions.q: Many microservices share one Postgres. Where does PgBouncer-style pooling belong?
options: Inside each service only, since a middle hop adds latency that outweighs any benefit
On developer machines, to catch connection leaks before production
Only in front of read replicas, never the primary
As a shared pooler before the database, with modest client-side pools

questions.q: A handler checks out a connection, calls a slow external API, then queries. Consequence?
options: The pool force-closes the connection after a fixed grace period
The connection sits idle mid-request, shrinking effective capacity
Postgres kills idle-in-transaction sessions immediately by default
Nothing, because pools transparently multiplex idle connections to other callers

questions.q: A service issues 1,000 queries/second, each holding a connection about 5 ms. Steady-state busy connections needed (Little's law)?
options: About 50
About 500
About 5
About 200

questions.q: During failover, every instance reconnects at once. What secondary failure threatens, and the usual defense?
options: Split-brain writes to two primaries; defend with synchronous replication everywhere
WAL corruption on the standby; defend with page checksums
Nothing serious, since the new primary accepts connections serially
A reconnect storm crushing the new primary; jittered backoff plus caps

questions.q: In benchmarks, a ~10-connection pool can beat a 100-connection pool on identical hardware. Why?
options: Plan caches hold about ten entries per backend by default
Smaller pools skip the TCP and TLS handshakes that larger pools must repeat
Past hardware parallelism, extra connections only add contention and switching
The OS scheduler throttles any process owning many sockets

questions.q: Under PgBouncer transaction mode, a client runs SET search_path, then queries in a later transaction. Risk?
options: The later query may land on a different server connection lacking that setting
PgBouncer rejects session-level SET statements outright in transaction mode
The SET is broadcast to every pooled server connection at once
Postgres raises an error because search_path needs session pooling

questions.q: A leaked connection sits 'idle in transaction' overnight. Effect on Postgres MVCC?
options: None, because idle transactions consume no server resources at all
Vacuum can't clear dead rows visible to its snapshot; bloat grows
It blocks all writes to every table the transaction previously read
WAL archiving pauses entirely until that transaction commits
